title: Arm's Length Relationship - Canadian SR&ED Tax Glossary
description: Learn how an Arm's Length Relationship affects subcontractor and third-party expenditures in our Canadian SR&ED tax credit glossary.
summary: An arm's-length relationship determines how SR&ED contract costs are treated under Canada's Income Tax Act. When a claimant pays an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor, 100% of eligible costs enter the section 37 pool but only 80% qualify for the investment tax credit, while non-arm's-length (related-party) contract payments earn the payer no ITC.

1. Executive Legislative Architecture and Statutory Foundations
1.1 Historical Evolution and Statutory Dual-Incentive Structure

The Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program constitutes the single largest federal source of financial support for industrial research and experimental development in Canada, providing statutory tax incentives to more than 24,160 businesses annually. The statutory lineage of Canadian research and development tax relief traces back to 1944 amendments to the Income War Tax Act—the legislative predecessor to the modern Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), hereinafter the "ITA")—which first permitted Canadian corporations to deduct research expenditures against business revenue notwithstanding the general statutory prohibition against capital and non-current outlays codified in section 18 of the ITA. The modern architecture of the SR&ED investment tax credit was introduced in 1983 and structurally consolidated in the May 23, 1985 federal budget papers (Securing Economic Renewal), tabled in the House of Commons by the Honourable Michael H. Wilson, Minister of Finance. This framework established a volume-based, two-pronged statutory incentive administered jointly by the Department of Finance Canada, which retains legislative and tax policy authority, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which exercises operational, technical, and financial audit authority.

Unlike single-tier super-deduction regimes utilized in several foreign jurisdictions, the Canadian federal SR&ED framework operates through two distinct, cumulative statutory mechanisms under the ITA that provide both an immediate or deferred income deduction and a direct tax credit. The first mechanism is the Section 37 Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool. Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures—and, for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, eligible capital SR&ED expenditures—incurred in Canada, along with limited permissible foreign SR&ED salary expenditures governed by subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5). This pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures may be deducted in full or in part to reduce taxable business income in the current taxation year, or carried forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. The second mechanism is the Section 127 and Section 127.1 Investment Tax Credit (ITC). Under subsections 127(5) through 127(10.2) and section 127.1 of the ITA, a taxpayer earns a volume-based Investment Tax Credit calculated as a flat statutory percentage—either the enhanced 35% rate or the basic 15% rate—of its "qualified expenditure" pool for the taxation year. Depending on the legal classification of the corporate claimant, its prior-year taxable capital or gross revenue, and whether the underlying outlay is current or capital in nature, the resulting ITC either reduces federal Part I tax otherwise payable or is paid out directly to the taxpayer as an immediate cash refund.

The interplay between the section 37 expenditure pool and the section 127 investment tax credit is governed by strict statutory anti-double-dipping mechanics designed to ensure that a taxpayer does not simultaneously receive both a tax-free cash credit and an unadjusted income deduction on the same dollar of expenditure. Any federal SR&ED ITC claimed in a given taxation year—whether applied to offset Part I tax payable or received as a cash refund—reduces the taxpayer's section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year; to the extent that this reduction would cause the section 37 pool balance to become negative, the negative balance is included directly in the taxpayer's taxable business income under paragraph 12(1)(t) of the ITA. Similarly, under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA, any provincial or territorial R&D tax credits, innovation grants, or other government or non-government assistance that a taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing date must be deducted directly from both the section 37 expenditure pool and the section 127 qualified expenditure base in the taxation year in which the expenditure is incurred.
1.2 The 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation: From the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15

Between 2024 and 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent its most expansive structural modernization in over a decade, reversing the austerity contractions that had been enacted in the 2012 federal budget and implemented in 2014. Because legislative proposals evolved significantly between initial consultation papers and final Parliamentary enactment, tax auditors and corporate practitioners must carefully distinguish the three policy stages of this reform when auditing or preparing claims spanning the 2024, 2025, and 2026 taxation years.

The first stage commenced on January 31, 2024, when the Department of Finance Canada launched Phase One of formal public consultations on modernizing the SR&ED program (running through April 15, 2024), seeking stakeholder input on program architecture, eligibility definitions, intellectual property retention within Canada, and complementarity with direct innovation support programs. In Budget 2024 (Fairness for Every Generation, tabled on April 16, 2024), the federal government initiated Phase Two of the consultations (running until May 27, 2024) and initially earmarked $600 million over four years commencing in 2025–2026, with $150 million per year ongoing, to fund prospective SR&ED enhancements.

The second stage occurred on December 16, 2024, with the tabling of the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), in which the federal government expanded its fiscal commitment to $1.9 billion over six years and announced four foundational reforms intended to take effect for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024). In that December 2024 FES announcement, the Department of Finance initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit on which the enhanced 35% credit can be earned from $3 million to $4.5 million (which would have provided qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporations with up to $1.575 million per year in refundable enhanced credits), raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, extending eligibility for the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs for property acquired or lease amounts first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024.

The third and definitive legislative stage unfolded in Budget 2025 and culminated in the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1). Rather than enacting the interim $4.5 million expenditure limit proposed in the 2024 FES, Budget 2025 doubled the annual enhanced expenditure limit directly from $3 million to $6,000,000. This $6 million expenditure limit—alongside the $15 million to $75 million taxable capital phase-out range, the extension of the 35% enhanced refundable credit to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations, and the restoration of capital expenditure and equipment lease eligibility—was formally enacted into law when Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Under the transitional and coming-into-force provisions of Bill C-15, these reforms apply retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (i.e., on or after December 16, 2024), while the restoration of capital property and lease cost eligibility applies to depreciable property acquired and available for use, or lease payments first becoming payable, after December 15, 2024.

body.text: A critical compliance nuance resulting from the enactment of Bill C-15 is the emergence of statutory cap divergences between the federal SR&ED regime and provincial R&D tax credit statutes. While Bill C-15 doubled the federal enhanced expenditure limit to $6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, provincial statutes that maintain independent statutory expenditure limits—most notably the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), whose annual expenditure limit remains fixed at $3 million—do not automatically track the federal increase. Consequently, corporate tax planners must model distinct marginal recovery rates across the $0 to $3 million, $3 million to $6 million, and above-$6 million expenditure bands.
1.3 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The statutory gateway to both the section 37 deduction pool and the section 127 investment tax credit is the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. While this definition generally conforms to the international standards of the OECD Frascati Manual, it imposes specific statutory inclusions and exclusions under Canadian domestic law. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four qualifying pillars.

The first qualifying pillar under paragraph 248(1)(a) is basic research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Because basic research is predominantly conducted within universities and specialized research institutes, it represents the smallest share of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada. The second pillar under paragraph 248(1)(b) is applied research, which encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. The third and commercially dominant pillar under paragraph 248(1)(c) is experimental development, defined as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development accounts for the vast majority of Canadian manufacturing, software engineering, and industrial SR&ED claims, and explicitly encompasses "shop floor SR&ED" conducted directly within a commercial production environment rather than an isolated laboratory. The fourth pillar under paragraph 248(1)(d) comprises eligible support work, which covers work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Simultaneously, paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) of the ITA explicitly exclude specific categories of commercial, routine, or non-scientific activity from the definition of SR&ED, even where such activities occur concurrently with an eligible innovation project. Specifically, SR&ED never includes market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes (such as user interface redesigns or aesthetic modifications); or routine data collection.

body.text: 2. Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Thresholds, and Corporate Eligibility Mechanics
2.1 Enhanced 35% Rate versus Basic 15% Rate Architecture

The Canadian federal SR&ED program operates on two flat statutory credit rates—an enhanced rate of 35% and a basic (general) rate of 15%—rather than a sliding percentage scale. Which rate applies to a given dollar of qualified SR&ED expenditure is governed by the legal status of the claimant and whether the expenditure falls within the claimant's annual expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA.

body.text: To qualify as a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) under subsections 125(7) and 248(1) of the ITA, a corporation must satisfy four cumulative conditions throughout the taxation year: first, it must be a private corporation; second, it must be a corporation that was resident in Canada and was either incorporated in Canada or resident in Canada continuously from June 18, 1971, to the end of the taxation year; third, it must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (encompassing both de jure voting control and de facto control under subsection 256(5.1)), by one or more non-resident persons, by one or more public corporations (other than a prescribed venture capital corporation), by one or more corporations listed on a designated stock exchange, or by any combination thereof; and fourth, no class of its shares of capital stock may be listed on a designated stock exchange. Furthermore, anti-avoidance rules governing "substantive CCPCs" (designed to tax passive investment income at CCPC rates) do not confer CCPC status for purposes of claiming the enhanced 35% SR&ED investment tax credit where corporate structures are manipulated.
2.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital and Gross Revenue Tests

Under subsection 127(10.2) of the ITA, as amended by Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the baseline annual SR&ED expenditure limit for a CCPC—or for an associated group of CCPCs, which must allocate the shared expenditure limit across the corporate group on Schedule T2SCH49—is $6,000,000.

Prior to the 2019 federal budget, the federal SR&ED expenditure limit was subject to a dual phase-out triggered by both prior-year taxable income ($500,000 to $800,000) and prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada ($10 million to $50 million). While the federal prior-year taxable income phase-out of the expenditure limit itself was repealed in 2019 (although prior-year qualifying income limits continue to determine whether a CCPC is an "excluded corporation" for purposes of refunding basic 15% credits), the taxable capital phase-out remained a major threshold for capital-intensive scaling firms. Under Bill C-15, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the taxable capital phase-out thresholds were increased from the $10 million–$50 million range to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, respectively.

Specifically, where TC represents the aggregate taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning of Part I.3 of the ITA, sections 181.2 to 181.4) of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year, a corporation whose prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less retains the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Where TC exceeds $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 baseline limit is phased out on a straight-line basis at the rate of $0.10 for each $1 of the excess of TC over $15,000,000, so that the expenditure limit equals $6,000,000 × ($60,000,000 − (TC − $15,000,000)) ÷ $60,000,000.

Once prior-year taxable capital reaches or exceeds $75,000,000 (TC ≥ $75,000,000), the federal expenditure limit is eliminated ($0), and the corporation may claim only the basic 15% non-refundable federal ITC on its qualified SR&ED expenditures. In addition, under the Bill C-15 amendments, a CCPC may elect to determine its expenditure limit phase-out using the three-year average gross revenue phase-out formula (the same metric applied to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations) instead of the Part I.3 taxable capital formula. This election provides substantial relief to capital-intensive clean technology, semiconductor, biotechnology, and hardware CCPCs that raise large equity or debt financing rounds—which inflate Part I.3 taxable capital—while still generating low or pre-commercial gross revenues.
2.3 Extension of the Enhanced Refundable Regime to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)

Historically, the moment a Canadian technology or life sciences enterprise completed an Initial Public Offering (IPO) or reverse takeover (RTO) on the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX), TSX Venture Exchange (TSXV), or Cboe Canada, it ceased to be a CCPC and immediately lost access to the 35% refundable SR&ED tax credit, dropping to the 15% non-refundable rate. For pre-profit public biotechnology, medical device, and clean-tech issuers with zero Part I corporate income tax payable, losing refundability meant that their SR&ED credits accumulated in non-refundable carryforward pools with no immediate cash-flow benefit.

To eliminate this statutory penalty against domestic public listings, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement and Bill C-15 extended the 35% enhanced refundable SR&ED ITC on up to $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Under the enacted definition, a corporation qualifies as an ECPC for a taxation year if it satisfies three statutory criteria throughout the taxation year: first, the corporation is resident in Canada; second, the corporation has a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange or has validly elected (or been designated by the Minister) to be a public corporation; and third, the corporation is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons.

For an ECPC, the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit is phased out on a straight-line basis using a three-year average gross revenue test aggregated across the associated corporate group over the three preceding taxation years. This mechanism ensures that pre-revenue and emerging public Canadian innovators receive up to $2.1 million annually in refundable cash credits, while profitable large-cap public corporations gradually transition to the standard 15% non-refundable credit as their commercial revenues scale.
2.4 Refundability Rules, Section 37 Deduction Pools, and Carryover Provisions

Under section 127.1 of the ITA, the cash refundability of an SR&ED ITC depends on the intersection of the claimant's corporate classification, whether the expenditure falls within or above the $6 million expenditure limit, and whether the underlying outlay is a current expenditure or a capital expenditure. For qualifying CCPCs (that are not "excluded corporations" by virtue of exceeding their prior-year qualifying income limit) and ECPCs, the enhanced 35% ITC earned on current expenditures up to the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is 100% refundable in cash. Thus, a pre-revenue Canadian startup or qualifying public company incurring $6,000,000 in qualifying current SR&ED expenditures with zero Part I tax payable receives a direct cash refund cheque or electronic deposit of $2,100,000 from the CRA.

By contrast, where a qualifying CCPC or ECPC incurs eligible capital expenditures (for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024) within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit, the enhanced 35% ITC earned on those capital expenditures is 40% refundable. For instance, $1,000,000 of eligible SR&ED capital expenditures within the expenditure limit generates a $350,000 enhanced ITC; if the corporation has no Part I tax payable, 40% of that credit ($140,000) is refunded in cash, while the remaining 60% ($210,000) is retained as a non-refundable ITC carryforward.

For current expenditures incurred above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit, a qualifying CCPC (whose prior-year taxable income does not exceed its qualifying income limit) earns the basic 15% ITC, of which 40% is refundable in cash (yielding an effective cash refund of 6% on current spend above $6 million, with the remaining 9% carried forward). For example, if a qualifying CCPC incurs $8,000,000 in eligible current SR&ED expenditures in its 2026 taxation year, the first $6,000,000 earns $2,100,000 at 35% (100% refundable) and the next $2,000,000 earns $300,000 at 15% (40% refundable = $120,000), resulting in $2,220,000 in total cash refunds and $180,000 in non-refundable ITC carryforwards. For ECPCs spending above their expenditure limit, and for all foreign-controlled corporations or non-qualifying public corporations, the 15% basic ITC is 100% non-refundable. Under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, any non-refundable portion of an SR&ED ITC that cannot be utilized to offset Part I tax payable in the current taxation year may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years.
3. Qualifying Expenditures, Cost Allocation Rules, and Restoration of Capital Eligibility

To earn an SR&ED investment tax credit, an expenditure must first constitute an allowable SR&ED expenditure under section 37 of the ITA (or be added via the Prescribed Proxy Amount under subsection 127(9) and Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations) and must be directly linked to eligible SR&ED project work carried on in Canada.

body.text: 3.1 Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged Labour, Specified Employees, and Foreign Work Limits

Employee salaries and wages represent the foundational expenditure category for most Canadian SR&ED claims, particularly across the software engineering, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced manufacturing sectors. Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA and CRA administrative policy, only remuneration paid to T4 employees—including the employer's share of statutory payroll levies such as Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Québec Pension Plan (QPP), Employment Insurance (EI), and provincial workers' compensation or health payroll taxes—qualifies as SR&ED salary or wages. If a company founder performs hands-on technical R&D work, the founder's remuneration is eligible only if the founder is compensated as a T4 employee on corporate payroll rather than through dividends or contractor drawings, and the CRA closely scrutinizes founder salaries that exceed fair market compensation rates. Furthermore, under the unpaid remuneration rule in subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any salary or wages accrued at year-end must be actually paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred; any portion remaining unpaid on the 181st day is disallowed for that taxation year and may be claimed only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually disbursed.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, employee labour qualifies as "directly engaged" in SR&ED across three distinct operational categories. The first category covers hands-on scientific or technical execution by engineers, software developers, scientists, and technicians who directly formulate hypotheses, design experiments, write experimental source code, construct prototypes, and analyse test results. The second category covers specific hands-on tasks performed by non-specialized employees—such as operating a production machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into an experimental line—provided those tasks are directly supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications. The third category covers technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the taxation year, such as planning for the assignment of technological personnel, job priorities, the development of technological strategies, and the quality of materials used. Conversely, administrative human resources, general corporate management, commercial product design, and non-technical project management are strictly excluded.

Stringent statutory caps apply to specified employees, defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as employees who are specified shareholders of the corporation (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who do not deal at arm's length with the corporation. For specified employees (whose allowable wages are reported on Line 315 of Form T661), all bonuses and any remuneration based on profits are 100% excluded, and total allowable SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days employed in the year. Moreover, when computing the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary base in Part 5 of Form T661, each specified employee's includable salary is further restricted to the lesser of 75% of their total salary and wages and 2.5 times the YMPE prorated for days employed in the taxation year. For a 2026 taxation year-end, this ceiling equals exactly $186,500 per specified employee.

With respect to SR&ED performed outside Canada, subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA permit a claimant to include foreign SR&ED wages in its Canadian SR&ED pool and ITC base only if four cumulative statutory conditions are met: first, the foreign SR&ED work must be performed directly by an employee of the taxpayer and never by a subcontractor; second, the employee must have been a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; third, the salary or wages paid for that work must not be subject to an income or profits tax imposed by another country; and fourth, the total permissible foreign SR&ED salary claimed cannot exceed 10% of the total SR&ED salaries and wages claimed for SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year.
3.2 Overhead Allocation: The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) versus the Traditional Method

In Part 3, Section A of Form T661, a claimant must elect whether to calculate its SR&ED overhead using the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162). Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA, this election must be made on the initial Form T661 filed for the taxation year and is statutorily irrevocable for that taxation year once filed—it cannot be altered on an amended tax return or during a CRA audit.

The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Method (Line 160), governed by Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, is elected by the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants because it eliminates the burden of identifying, tracking, and allocating individual overhead expenses. Under the proxy method, the claimant calculates a notional substitute amount equal to 55% of its SR&ED salary base (entered on Line 818 and Line 820 of Part 5 of Form T661 and carried to Line 502 of Part 4). The salary base consists solely of the eligible salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (subject to the specified employee cap of $186,500 for 2026 and the overall proxy cap), and never includes subcontractor fees, taxable benefits, or clerical/support staff salaries. Because the PPA is a notional statutory amount created solely to compute the Section 127 qualified expenditure base for ITC purposes, the PPA cannot be included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures; instead, the claimant deducts its actual underlying overhead expenses—such as general-purpose office equipment or furniture, salaries of support or clerical staff, office supplies, and utilities—as ordinary business deductions under section 9 of the ITA.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method (Line 162), no 55% proxy is added. Instead, the claimant must specifically identify, track, and allocate actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly related to the SR&ED work and incremental—meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred if the SR&ED work had not occurred. While the traditional method requires rigorous accounting substantiation and is subject to detailed verification by CRA Financial Reviewers, it can yield a larger tax credit than the 55% PPA for facility-intensive or heavy industrial claimants whose incremental utilities, shop-floor support labour, and testing equipment maintenance exceed 55% of direct research payroll.
3.3 Materials Consumed or Transformed and Cloud Computing Infrastructure

Allowable material expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(a) of the ITA encompass the cost of raw materials, components, and supplies that are either consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually value-less) or transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype or pilot production run) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Materials used in commercial production do not qualify, and if an experimental prototype or transformed material whose cost was previously claimed for SR&ED is subsequently sold commercially or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules require the claimant to add back the lesser of the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value) and the original claimed cost to increase tax otherwise payable.

For modern software, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and DevOps enterprises, cloud computing and data processing expenses (such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), and Microsoft Azure compute instances, GPU clusters used for machine learning model training, and experimental data storage) constitute a vital component of eligible SR&ED project costs, typically claimed under materials consumed or directly related SR&ED expenditures. In alignment with CRA guidelines on cloud computing expenses, claimants must enforce strict accounting segmentation between commercial production hosting and R&D experimentation. Specifically, production cloud infrastructure hosting live customer applications and commercial third-party API calls represent Cost of Goods Sold (COGS / Cost of Revenue) and are completely ineligible for SR&ED. To substantiate cloud costs during a CRA audit, companies must maintain separate cloud accounts or export monthly AWS, GCP, and Azure billing reports with granular resource tags that segregate qualifying development, staging, and experimental testing environments from production workloads.
3.4 Subcontractor Payments, Non-Arm's-Length Transactions, and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts out SR&ED work, the ITA establishes distinct statutory rules for arm's-length Canadian contractors, non-arm's-length (related-party) contractors, foreign contractors, and approved third-party research entities.

Where a claimant pays an arm's-length subcontractor to perform eligible SR&ED work in Canada on the claimant's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract cost is included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure is included in the Section 127 qualified expenditure base for calculating the SR&ED ITC. This statutory 80% rule removes the subcontractor's presumed commercial profit markup from the ITC calculation. For example, if a qualifying CCPC pays an arm's-length Canadian machine learning specialist $140,000 for 100% qualifying SR&ED work in Canada, $112,000 ($140,000 × 80%) enters the qualified expenditure base, generating a $39,200 refundable federal ITC at the 35% rate. Only the technical SR&ED portion of a subcontractor's invoice qualifies; project management, UI design, and non-technical tasks must be excluded before applying the 80% factor, and all arm's-length contracts exceeding $30,000 must be listed on Line 340 of Form T661.

Where a claimant subcontracts SR&ED work to a non-arm's-length (related-party) contractor, the contract payment can be included in the payer's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, but it does not qualify for an ITC in the hands of the payer (0% ITC inclusion). Instead, the related party performing the SR&ED work in Canada may claim the ITC on its own underlying qualified SR&ED expenditures. Non-arm's-length contracts exceeding $30,000 must be itemized on Line 345 of Form T661. Furthermore, any contract for SR&ED performed outside Canada earns zero investment tax credit, as contracted SR&ED counts only when physically carried out in Canada. Finally, a claimant may claim third-party payments (included at 80% for ITC purposes) made to CRA-approved entities—including approved research associations, approved Canadian universities, colleges, and research institutes, approved granting councils, or tax-exempt Canadian resident non-profit SR&ED corporations—provided the SR&ED is carried out in Canada, relates to a business of the claimant, and the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the research.
3.5 Restored Capital Expenditures (CAPEX) and Equipment Lease Costs Post-December 15, 2024

One of the most impactful provisions enacted in Bill C-15 (following the 2024 Fall Economic Statement) is the restoration of capital expenditure and equipment lease cost eligibility for both the Section 37 deduction pool and the Section 127 ITC component, ending the 11-year exclusion that had been in place since January 1, 2014. Under the restored statutory rules, which generally mirror the pre-2014 regime and apply to depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, and equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, claimants can once again claim capital R&D investments.

To qualify as an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported on Line 390 of Form T661 Version 26), the expenditure must be made to acquire new or used depreciable property (such as specialized laboratory instruments, industrial prototyping machinery, testing apparatus, or local GPU compute servers) for which the claimant intends, at the time of acquisition, either that the property will be used in the performance of SR&ED in Canada for all or substantially all (90% or more) of its expected useful life, or that 90% or more of its value will be consumed in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. Land, buildings, and leasehold interests remain statutorily ineligible, and under the proxy method, general-purpose office equipment or furniture cannot be claimed as capital property because it is already covered by the 55% PPA. Claimants must keep any property claimed on Line 390 off Schedule 8 (Capital Cost Allowance) and maintain rigorous records of the acquisition date, available-for-use date, and SR&ED usage logs. As noted in Section 2.4, enhanced 35% ITCs earned on capital expenditures up to the $6 million expenditure limit are 40% refundable for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs.

With respect to equipment lease costs, amounts first becoming payable after December 15, 2024, to lease equipment used 90% or more for SR&ED in Canada are 100% eligible (reported on Line 350 of Form T661, excluding general-purpose office equipment or furniture under the proxy method). Additionally, where a claimant elects the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) method, if leased equipment (other than general-purpose office equipment or furniture) is used between 50% and under 90% for SR&ED in Canada, half (50%) of the lease costs are eligible and reported on Line 355 of Form T661.
3.6 Government Assistance, Non-Commercial Loans, and Prescribed Exclusions

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to 127(20) of the ITA, both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure base must be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED at the time the tax return is filed. Government assistance encompasses direct innovation grants (such as NRC IRAP or CanExport SMEs), forgivable loans, concessional non-commercial government loans (such as unsecured SADI loans adjudicated in CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178), and all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (including the Ontario OITC/ORDTC/OBRITC, Quebec CRIC, BC SR&ED credit, and Alberta IEG). If government or non-government assistance that previously reduced a claimant's SR&ED pool is subsequently repaid, the repayment is entered on Line 445 of Form T661 (and Schedule B) to restore the deductible pool and reclaim the lost SR&ED ITCs in the year of repayment.

Finally, under the CRA's Total Qualified Expenditures Policy, professional or contingency fees paid to consultants, accounting firms, or tax lawyers to prepare and file an SR&ED claim (which typically range from 15% to 20% of the approved credit in the contingency market) are prescribed expenditures that must be subtracted in Part 4 of Form T661. While such claim-preparation fees may be deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA, they never earn an SR&ED investment tax credit.
4. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Multi-Jurisdictional Stacking

Across Canada, nine provinces and the Yukon Territory operate statutory R&D tax credit or grant programs that stack with the federal SR&ED incentive. Except for Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), provincial and territorial R&D credits are harmonized with the federal SR&ED definition under subsection 248(1) and are processed directly by the CRA alongside the federal T2 return.

body.text: 4.1 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC Divergence from the Federal $6 Million Limit

Ontario administers three distinct R&D tax credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all processed by the CRA since December 31, 2008. The primary refundable incentive for small and medium-sized enterprises is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; previously 10%) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual Ontario expenditure limit of $3,000,000. Although the 2018 Ontario Budget had proposed an R&D-intensity sliding scale between 8% and 12% and some secondary commentary misstates the rate, the enacted OITC rate administered by the CRA is 8%. Corporate tax auditors must account for two critical divergences between Ontario's OITC and the post-Bill C-15 federal SR&ED regime: first, Ontario's OITC expenditure limit remains fixed at $3,000,000 and does not match the federal Bill C-15 increase to $6,000,000, meaning that qualified Ontario spending between $3 million and $6 million earns the 35% federal credit without the 8% OITC top-up; second, unlike the federal expenditure limit (which repealed its taxable income phase-out in 2019), the Ontario expenditure limit continues to phase out on a straight-line basis when the associated group's prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when prior-year taxable paid-up capital is between $25 million and $50 million.

Alongside the OITC, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; previously 4.5%) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures. Once a corporation's Ontario expenditure limit is eliminated due to prior-year taxable income exceeding $800,000, or on expenditures exceeding $3 million, it may claim the 3.5% ORDTC. Because both the OITC and the ORDTC constitute government assistance that reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool, an unprofitable corporation that cannot utilize the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC to offset Ontario corporate income tax should consider delivering a formal written Waiver of Tax Credit with its tax return (on or before six months after its taxation year-end, or on an amended return) so that the unusable 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC does not grind down its 35% cash-refundable federal SR&ED ITC. Finally, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred under eligible contracts with approved Ontario research institutes (universities, colleges, and hospital research institutes), subject to a $20,000,000 annual expenditure cap.
4.2 Quebec: The 2025–2026 Budget Overhaul, CRIC Implementation, CDAEIA, DICI, and C3i

In the 2025–2026 Quebec Budget (Innover pour prospérer, tabled by Finance Minister Éric Girard on March 25, 2025) and detailed in Revenu Québec's Fiscal News Bulletin published on July 9, 2025, the Government of Quebec enacted a comprehensive structural overhaul of its innovation tax regime, committing $271.5 million in additional financial support over five years. Concluding that its previous framework of nine separate innovation tax measures had become overly complex and uncompetitive after the 2014 rate cuts and multiple fragmented exclusion thresholds, Quebec abolished eight legacy measures—including the flagship R&D Salary Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.7, which provided a 14% base to 30% enhanced refundable credit for taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025), the research consortium tax credit, the private partnership pre-competitive research credit, the technological adaptation services credit, the industrial design tax credit, and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts—and consolidated them into the CRIC (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation).

The CRIC applies to taxation years or fiscal periods of a corporation or partnership that begin after March 25, 2025. Consequently, a corporation whose taxation year began on January 1, 2025, and ended on December 31, 2025, cannot claim the CRIC for 2025 (it continues to claim the legacy R&D salary tax credit on Form RD-1029.7 for 2025) and transitions to the CRIC (claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T with the CO-17 return within 18 months of fiscal year-end) starting with its taxation year beginning January 1, 2026. Crucially, CCPC status is not used for the CRIC: any eligible corporation with an establishment in Quebec—whether a CCPC startup, a public company, or a foreign-owned multinational subsidiary—earns a 100% refundable tax credit of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures exceeding its exclusion threshold, and 20% on all eligible expenditures beyond that first $1,000,000.

While keeping its definition of R&D harmonized with the federal SR&ED program, the CRIC significantly broadens the scope of eligible expenditures in two ways. First, it covers pre-commercialization activities performed in Quebec—such as technological validation, regulatory testing, and certification or homologation studies—even if those pre-commercialization activities follow up on an R&D project conducted prior to March 25, 2025. Second, it restores eligibility for capital expenditures (CAPEX) on equipment acquired for R&D or pre-commercialization in Quebec at the identical 30% / 20% refundable rates. Under the CRIC, employee salaries and capital equipment enter the eligible base at 100%, while eligible subcontracting contracts (such as with universities, public research centres, or CCTTs) are eligible at 50%. To focus fiscal assistance on high-value-added employment, a claimant's total eligible expenditures must exceed a modified single exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the applicable Basic Personal Amount under the Quebec personal income tax system ($18,571 for 2025) multiplied by the proportion of time each employee devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities during the year.

For example, a Quebec corporation with 3 full-time R&D employees (100% time for 12 months) and 2 employees devoting 75% of their time to R&D for 6 months in a 2025-start year has an employee-based threshold of (3 × $18,571) + (2 × 75% × 6/12 × $18,571) = $69,641, which exceeds the $50,000 floor and serves as its single exclusion threshold.

Complementing the CRIC, Quebec updated three related innovation and investment incentives. First, for fiscal years beginning after December 31, 2025, the legacy E-Business Development Tax Credit (CDAE, which provided a 30% IT salary credit split 24% refundable / 6% non-refundable in 2024, and 23% refundable / 7% non-refundable in 2025) is replaced by the CDAEIA (Crédit d'impôt pour le développement des affaires électroniques intégrant l'intelligence artificielle). Requiring an annual eligibility certificate from Investissement Québec confirming that the corporation integrates artificial intelligence features in a significant way, the CDAEIA provides a 30% credit on eligible AI/IT salaries above an exclusion threshold, structured as 22% refundable + 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% refundable + 9% non-refundable in 2027, and 20% refundable + 10% non-refundable from 2028 onward (with strict anti-cumulation rules prohibiting a taxpayer from claiming both CRIC and CDAEIA on the same salary expense). Second, Quebec retained the DICI (Déduction incitative pour la commercialisation des innovations), an IP Box deduction that lowers the effective Quebec corporate income tax rate from 11.5% to 2% on eligible taxable income (including sales, royalties, and judicial patent infringement damages) derived from commercializing qualifying intellectual property assets developed significantly in Quebec. Third, the C3i (Crédit d'impôt pour investissement et innovation) provides a 100% refundable credit (for taxation years beginning after 2023) of 15%, 20%, or 25% by regional economic vitality on eligible manufacturing equipment, computer hardware, and management software above $5,000 or $12,500 per property, up to a $100 million four-year cap.
4.3 Western Canada: British Columbia, Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan

Across Western Canada, four distinct provincial frameworks incentivize R&D. In British Columbia, the CRA administers the BC SR&ED Tax Credit, which provides a 10% tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in British Columbia; this 10% credit is 100% refundable for qualifying CCPCs up to their expenditure limit and non-refundable for non-CCPCs or expenditures above the limit.

In Alberta, for eligible R&D expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020 (matching those that qualify for the federal SR&ED program), the province operates the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), which must be claimed within 15 months after the corporation's filing due date. Capped at $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending, the IEG provides qualified corporations with an 8% base refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (its prior two-year average Alberta R&D spend) and an enhanced 20% refundable payment on incremental Alberta R&D spending exceeding that base level.

In Manitoba, the CRA administers the Manitoba R&D Tax Credit, which equals 15% of eligible Manitoba R&D expenditures made after April 11, 2017 (down from the prior 20% rate). One-half of the credit on in-house R&D (7.5%) is immediately refundable in cash and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable, whereas R&D conducted under contract with an eligible research institute is 100% refundable (15%). In Saskatchewan, the CRA administers the Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit, which provides a 10% tax credit that is 100% refundable for CCPCs on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures and non-refundable above $1,000,000 or for non-CCPCs.
4.4 Atlantic Canada and Northern Territories: Refundable Regimes in NS, NB, NL, and Yukon

The Atlantic provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Newfoundland and Labrador, together with the Yukon Territory, provide a 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit administered by the CRA on eligible SR&ED expenditures carried out within their respective borders. Unlike Ontario, British Columbia, or Saskatchewan, these four jurisdictions extend 100% cash refundability to all corporations—regardless of whether the claimant is a CCPC, a public company, or a foreign-owned subsidiary—with no annual expenditure ceiling.
4.5 Mathematical Modelling of Federal-Provincial Assistance Grind and Pool Recapture

Because provincial R&D tax credits and the Alberta IEG constitute government assistance under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the ITA, they reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool prior to calculating the 35% or 15% federal SR&ED ITC. Consequently, a founder or tax director cannot simply add the nominal provincial rate to the 35% federal rate; instead, where Q represents gross federal qualified expenditures, p represents the effective provincial credit rate on Q, and f represents the federal ITC rate, the combined net tax credit recovery is governed by the interaction formula Q × [p + f × (1 − p)].

The following table models three comprehensive 2026 corporate scenarios demonstrating how the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA), the provincial government assistance grind, Ontario's $3 million OITC cap divergence from the $6 million federal Bill C-15 cap, and Quebec's new CRIC exclusion threshold operate mathematically:

body.text: As these calculations demonstrate, the notional 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount creates a powerful multiplier on direct Canadian R&D salary outlays. In British Columbia (Scenario A), $645,161 of direct R&D salaries generates a $1,000,000 qualified expenditure base and $415,000 in combined cash refunds—representing a 64.33% cash recovery on actual salary expenditure. In Ontario (Scenario B), because the 8% OITC applies only to the first $3,000,000 of qualified expenditures ($240,000 OITC) while the federal 35% credit applies to the full $6,000,000 less $240,000 ($5,760,000 × 35% = $2,016,000), a qualifying CCPC spending $6,000,000 recovers $2,256,000 in cash (or slightly over $2.26 million if also utilizing the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC against Ontario tax payable), yielding a blended recovery rate of roughly 37.6% to 38% on the $6 million proxy-inclusive base rather than the 43% a founder might mistakenly expect. In Quebec (Scenario C), a corporation employing 10 full-time R&D engineers at $100,000 each ($1,000,000 direct payroll) earns $244,287 under the 30% CRIC (after deducting the $185,710 employee exclusion threshold) plus $457,000 in federal SR&ED refunds (35% of the $1,550,000 proxy-adjusted base minus $244,287 CRIC assistance), recovering $701,287 in cash—or 70.13% of its out-of-pocket R&D salary outlay.
5. Administrative Governance, Form T661 (Version 26) Compliance, and Audit Procedures
5.1 CRA Governance, Pre-Claim Consultation, and Review Timelines

The federal SR&ED program is administered by the Canada Revenue Agency through specialized SR&ED Coordinating Tax Services Offices (CTSOs). The CRA aims to process refundable SR&ED claims within 60 to 120 days of filing when accepted without audit, or within 120 to 180 days when selected for a technical and financial review. Across the 2023–2024 fiscal year, 91% of SR&ED claims were accepted by the CRA either as filed or with minor modifications. For businesses seeking upfront eligibility certainty prior to filing their return, the CRA provides a Pre-Claim Consultation and Pre-Claim Approval service, available for the 2026 taxation year to corporate applicants whose gross business income is below $25,000,000.

When a claim is selected for review (which occurs frequently for first-time claimants or large claims), the audit is conducted jointly by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), who evaluates the scientific or technological eligibility of each project under subsection 248(1) and conducts technical interviews with the claimant's CTO or lead engineers, and a Financial Reviewer (FR), who audits payroll records, time allocations, subcontractor contracts, cloud computing logs, and capital asset usage.
5.2 Line-by-Line Technical and Financial Architecture of Form T661 (Version 26) and Schedule T2SCH31

Following the enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA published Version 26 of Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), updated on May 15, 2026, which must be filed alongside Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) and interpreted using CRA Guide T4088 and the CRA's interim instructions for restored capital and lease lines.

body.text: 5.3 The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline and Statute-Barred Risks

Under subsections 37(11) and 127(9) of the ITA, both Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 must be filed within 12 months after the corporation's T2 filing due date. Because a corporation's T2 income tax return is due 6 months after the end of its taxation year under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA, the statutory filing deadline for an SR&ED claim is exactly 18 months after the end of the taxation year. For example, for a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end, the T2 return is due June 30, 2025, and the absolute deadline to file or amend Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 is June 30, 2026. For a partnership, the partnership itself must file a single Form T661 reporting all of its SR&ED expenditures, and individual partners cannot add partnership SR&ED expenditures to their own pools.

This 18-month filing deadline is an absolute statutory bar. The CRA does not grant administrative extensions, and if a claimant forgets to report an expenditure or project on its original Form T661, an amended Form T661 adding that expenditure or project can be submitted only before the 18-month deadline expires. Any project or expenditure line item omitted after the 18-month mark is permanently disallowed by operation of subsection 37(11).
5.4 Contemporaneous Documentation Standards and RTA/FR Audit Defence Protocols

The CRA requires evidence that SR&ED work was documented during the project as the work progressed, rather than reconstructed at year-end. To defend a claim successfully during an RTA and FR review, claimants should establish an integrated documentation workflow at project onboarding that captures both technical and financial records corresponding to Lines 270–282 of Form T661. On the technical side, this includes dated records of the technological uncertainty identified at the start of the project, architecture decision records (ADRs), experiment logs, sprint notes flagged for SR&ED, Git commit histories, Jira or Linear tickets, and test benchmark data—including failed experiments, which fully qualify so long as they form part of a systematic investigation. On the financial side, claimants must maintain monthly developer timesheets coded to specific SR&ED project identifiers, payroll registers, purchase orders and material invoices, written subcontractor contracts specifying Canadian SR&ED tasks, segmented cloud computing billing exports, and capital asset acquisition and usage logs.
6. Judicial Precedents and Tax Court / Federal Court of Appeal Jurisprudence

Over the past three decades—and with heightened intensity between 2021 and 2025—the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA), and the Supreme Court of Canada (SCC) have established a definitive body of case law governing technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) and financial assistance adjustments under section 127 of the ITA.

headers: Judicial Holding & Precedential Impact on SR&ED Audits

cells: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)
Statutory interpretation of "scientific research and experimental development" under s. 248(1) ITA.

Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman established the canonical Five-Question Legal Test at para. 16: (1) Technological risk/uncertainty; (2) Formulation of hypotheses; (3) Adherence to the total discipline of the scientific method; (4) Technological advancement; and (5) Detailed contemporaneous record-keeping.
Evidentiary weight of Question 5 of Northwest Hydraulic (contemporaneous documentation).

Allowed the taxpayer's appeal; held that once the trial judge had found that testing had been carried out and had produced a technological advance, he erred in denying the claim for lack of documented test results capable of making the tests repeatable.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88
Whether adherence to the "scientific method" (Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic) is mandatory given that the phrase does not appear in s. 248(1) ITA.
Unanimously dismissed the taxpayer's appeal; reaffirmed that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria—including adherence to the scientific method—are the binding legal interpretation of s. 248(1).
National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47; SCC leave dismissed Mar 9, 2023, No. 40303)
Tax Court (2020), Federal Court of Appeal (2022), Supreme Court of Canada (2023)
Whether applied science / software engineering is exempt from the "scientific method" test, and admissibility of expert reports seeking to redefine SR&ED methodology.

FCA (Rennie J.A.) upheld Lafleur J.'s disallowance where records were "vague" and "unclear"; rejected any distinction between natural and applied sciences unless proven in fact, and barred expert witnesses from acting as advocates or redefining the legal test; SCC denied leave with costs.
CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178 (aff'g 2021 TCC 57)
Tax Court (2021), Federal Court of Appeal (2022)
Whether an $81.6M unsecured, unconditionally repayable federal loan under the SADI program constituted "government assistance" reducing SR&ED ITCs and includable in income.

Held that because the loan terms were not "strictly commercial", the entire loan constituted government assistance that ground down CAE's SR&ED ITC pool (with relief available only at Line 445 of Form T661 as repayments are made) and triggered income inclusion (prompting a Nov 2023 FES legislative fix for the income side).
Eligibility of "shop floor SR&ED" in commercial food manufacturing (custom frozen pie recipe scaling across 2013–2016 tax years).

Ruled in favour of the taxpayer on $343,449+ of denied expenditures ($60,963+ ITCs); held that scaling food recipes to industrial freezing created genuine technological uncertainties not solvable by routine culinary techniques, and CEO testimony paired with iterative formulation logs satisfied Northwest Hydraulic.
DAZZM Inc. v. The King (Oct 2024, TCC) & Buehler Versatile Inc. v. The King (Feb 2023, TCC)
Distinction between complex routine software/industrial engineering and genuine technological uncertainty under s. 248(1).
Reinforced strict judicial scrutiny requiring taxpayers to isolate specific system-level technological uncertainties from complex but routine commercial product development.

body.text: 6.1 The Foundational Five-Part Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is the decision of Judge (later Chief Justice) Donald Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC). At paragraph 16 of his reasons, Justice Bowman articulated the five cumulative questions that Canadian courts and CRA auditors apply to determine whether claimed activities constitute SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA:

First, was there a technical risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? If the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering known to competent professionals in the field, no technological uncertainty exists. Second, did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This requires a five-stage methodology comprising the observation of the subject matter of the problem, the formulation of a clear objective, the identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, the formulation of an hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, and the methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. Third, did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?. Fourth, did the process result in a technological advancement, that is to say an advancement in the general understanding? (including the rejection of an hypothesis, which advances technological knowledge by ruling out a plausible approach). Fifth, although the Income Tax Act and the Regulations do not say so explicitly, did the taxpayer keep a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed?.

In August 2021, when the CRA archived its older Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and issued its updated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives, it structured these five questions into two overarching requirements derived from subsection 248(1): the "Why" requirement (why is the work being conducted—to advance scientific knowledge or achieve a technological advancement?) and the "How" requirement (how is the work being conducted—by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology through hypothesis generation, testing by experiment or analysis, logical conclusions, and contemporaneous evidence?).
6.2 Contemporaneous Evidence and Burden of Proof: RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal clarified the legal operation of the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic. The Tax Court had found that experimentation and testing had been carried out and had resulted in a technological advance in the construction industry, but denied the claim because the taxpayer's documentary evidence could not make the tests repeatable. The Federal Court of Appeal allowed the taxpayer's appeal, holding that once testing resulting in a technological advance had been established, the trial judge erred in imposing on the taxpayer the additional burden of proof of adducing documentary evidence of the test results.
6.3 Reaffirmation of the Scientific Method: Kam-Press Metal Products and National R&D Inc.

In two landmark appellate rulings—Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47, Lafleur J.; application for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed with costs on March 9, 2023, SCC Docket No. 40303)—the Federal Court of Appeal rejected taxpayer arguments that the third criterion of Northwest Hydraulic ("total discipline of the scientific method") should not apply because the words "scientific method" do not appear in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Writing for the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D, Justice Rennie held that Kam-Press had settled the law that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria represent the mandatory legal interpretation of subsection 248(1), upheld the trial judge's disallowance where the taxpayer's records were "vague," "unclear," and failed to show a logical progression between experimental premise and result, and barred the taxpayer from using an expert witness report as an advocate to argue "through the back door" that applied science or software engineering follows a looser methodology than natural science.
6.4 Concessional Government Loans as Assistance: CAE Inc. v. The King

In CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178 (October 19, 2022, aff'g 2021 TCC 57, September 14, 2021), the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal examined $81.6 million in unsecured, non-forgivable, unconditionally repayable loans received by Canadian aerospace firm CAE Inc. under the federal Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI). The courts held that because the loan terms were not "strictly commercial," the loans constituted government assistance that reduced CAE's SR&ED ITC pool dollar-for-dollar (with SR&ED ITCs recoverable only at Line 445 of Form T661 in future years as loan principal is repaid) and triggered immediate income inclusion. While the federal government proposed a legislative remedy in the November 21, 2023 Fall Economic Statement to address the unintended loans-as-income inclusion, the reduction of SR&ED qualified expenditure pools by concessional government financing remains a critical audit rule.
6.5 Industrial Scaling and Shop-Floor SR&ED: Canafric Inc. v. The King and Recent TCC Rulings

In Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108 (decided July 26, 2023), the Tax Court of Canada ruled in favour of a frozen pie manufacturer whose SR&ED claims across its 2013, 2014, 2015, and 2016 taxation years (totalling $343,449 in disclosed denied expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs across 2013, 2015, and 2016, plus three denied projects in 2014) had been disallowed by the CRA. The Tax Court accepted the detailed evidence of Canafric's CEO (Mr. Pandya) and held that scaling culinary recipes to industrial frozen pie production for retailers such as Costco and Loblaws created genuine technological uncertainties that could not be resolved by routine techniques, confirming that properly documented "shop floor SR&ED" in traditional food and manufacturing industries fully satisfies Northwest Hydraulic. Conversely, other recent Tax Court decisions—including Airzone One Ltd. v. The Queen (February 2022), Dave's Diesel Inc. v. The Queen (June 2022), JEC Distributors Inc. v. The King (December 2022), Buehler Versatile Inc. v. The King (February 2023), and DAZZM Inc. v. The King (October 2024)—underscore that claimants must rigorously isolate genuine technological uncertainties from routine engineering.
7. Strategic Compliance Conclusions and Audit Risk Mitigation Framework

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026 (retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024) and Quebec's 2025–2026 Budget transition to the CRIC and CDAEIA represent the most substantial expansion of Canadian R&D tax incentives in more than a decade. With the federal enhanced 35% expenditure limit doubled to $6,000,000, the taxable capital phase-out expanded to $15 million–$75 million, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations admitted to the 35% refundable credit, and capital equipment and lease eligibility restored after an 11-year absence, qualifying Canadian corporations can now recover up to $2.1 million annually in federal refundable cash credits on current expenditures alone.

To maximize recovery under this modernized statutory framework while insulating claims against CRA Research and Technology Advisor and Financial Reviewer audit adjustments, corporate claimants and tax auditors should integrate six core compliance practices into their annual tax cycle. First, Ontario claimants scaling between $3,000,000 and $6,000,000 of qualified expenditures must model the fact that Ontario's 8% refundable OITC remains capped at $3,000,000, and unprofitable Ontario claimants should evaluate filing a formal written Waiver of Tax Credit within 6 months of year-end so that the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC does not grind down their 35% cash-refundable federal SR&ED ITC. Second, Quebec corporations must align their fiscal year-start dates with the March 25, 2025 transition to the 30%/20% CRIC (Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, which includes pre-commercialization and capital equipment without requiring CCPC status) and the January 1, 2026 transition from the CDAE to the AI-focused CDAEIA, while preventing double-claiming of salaries across both credits. Third, when claiming restored capital expenditures on Line 390 of Form T661 (Version 26) for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, claimants must document SR&ED usage in Canada, exclude those assets from Schedule 8 (CCA), and account for the 40% refundability rule on enhanced capital ITCs. Fourth, financial controllers must model both the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 160, including the $186,500 specified employee PPA salary base cap for 2026 and the Line 355 50% lease rule) and the Traditional method (Line 162) before filing the initial T661 for the year, as that election is irrevocable under subsection 37(10). Fifth, software and AI startups must implement automated resource tagging on AWS, GCP, and Azure from day one to separate qualifying R&D staging and model-training environments from commercial production COGS, while ensuring all accrued SR&ED wages are paid within 180 days of year-end and all specified employee bonuses are excluded from Line 315. Finally, in light of the Federal Court of Appeal's uncompromising enforcement of the scientific method in Kam-Press (2021 FCA 88) and National R&D (2022 FCA 72), technical narratives in Part 2, Section B of Form T661 (within the 350-, 700-, and 350-word limits) must explicitly articulate the technological uncertainty, causal hypotheses, and systematic experimental testing results, backed by contemporaneous repositories and test logs ticked on Lines 270–282 and filed strictly before the 18-month statutory deadline.
